title: Samsung Electronics third-quarter profit in line with estimates amid rising demand for AI memory chips
content: South Korean tech giant Samsung Electronics on Thursday reported third-quarter operating profit that is broadly in line with analysts' expectations, as demand for advanced memory chips used in artificial intelligence applications continued to grow. Here are Samsung's third-quarter results compared with LSEG SmartEstimates, which are weighted toward forecasts from analysts who are more consistently accurate: Samsung's revenue rose 126.88% year-on-year and 13.85% from the previous quarter, while operating profit rose 783.11% from a year earlier. During the third quarter, Samsung Electronics and five of its affiliates announced a combined $1 billion investment in KKR-backed Helix Digital Infrastructure. Samsung Electronics will invest $500 million, with the remaining amount coming from its affiliates. Samsung also announced a partnership with French AI startup Mistral AI to use AI technologies in its semiconductor operations, including chip design and manufacturing. The company also led Mistral's Series D funding round.

title: As Waymo expands overseas, it remains a niche cash-burning business
content: Waymo is dominant in the U.S. and expanding overseas, but it remains immaterial in terms of revenue to parent Alphabet , which is pouring cash into its growth. In Alphabet's third-quarter earnings report on Wednesday, the company said its Other Bets segment, which includes Waymo, generated $372 million in revenue, up 8% from a year earlier, and accounting for just 0.3% of total sales. That revenue comes at a steep price. Operating loss in the Other Bets segment widened to $2.05 billion during the quarter from $1.43 billion a year ago. The unit also houses drug design research business Isomorphic, which is using Google's Gemini 4 Argon AI models. CEO Sundar Pichai touted Waymo's expansion toward the end of his introductory remarks on the earnings call. The company has a commanding lead in the U.S. robotaxi market, where it faces emerging competition from Amazon's Zoox and Tesla . Waymo said in August that it plans to roll out robotaxi rides in Germany in 2027, marking its third international market and first in the EU. "Waymo now operates in 15 major U.S. cities and just recently opened up service to the public in San Antonio, San Diego and Tampa with planned expansions into Canada, Germany, Singapore and Spain," Pichai said on the call. Waymo's steepest competition on the global stage comes from Baidu's Apollo Go, which is based in China. For years, Alphabet was able to operate Waymo as a side project while its core online ads business racked up tens of billions of dollars in annual profit and threw off mounds of cash. But with the company now investing heavily in artificial intelligence, free cash flow has turned negative and Wall Street has shown signs of concern. Alphabet reported an earnings and revenue miss on Wednesday, sending the stock down almost 10% in extended trading. The company maintained its full-year capital expenditures forecast at between $195 billion and $205 billion, largely for AI infrastructure, and reported negative free cash flow of over $9 billion for the quarter. Earlier this month, Waymo announced that it had closed a $5 ‌billion term loan, its first debt financing. In February, the robotaxi business announced that it had raised $16 billion at a $126 billion valuation in a funding round led by Alphabet that included support from Andreessen Horowitz, Fidelity, T. Rowe Price, Sequoia Capital, Kleiner Perkins and others. Last week Waymo started offering driverless rides to and from the Las Vegas airport, after previously announcing airport service in five other cities, including San Francisco and Phoenix. "Waymo is on a great trajectory," Pichai said on Wednesday. "We have now driven more than 300 million fully autonomous miles." Tesla says on its website that driverless vehicles in its Robotaxi network have completed about 3.8 million miles "unsupervised," or without a human driver at the wheel. CEO Elon Musk said on the company's earnings call last week that the Robotaxi business should become a "meaningful" revenue contributor by the second half of 2027. Monday - Friday, 6:00 - 7:00 PM ET CNBC's Jim Cramer said Wednesday that a handful of technology giants have become so powerful that their influence extends far beyond their stock prices. The " Mad Money " host likened them to "nation states," pointing to their dominant competitive positions, ability to generate substantial profits and willingness to aggressively invest in emerging technologies. Cramer identified Alphabet , Amazon , Apple , Meta Platforms , Microsoft , Nvidia , Tesla , SpaceX , Anthropic and OpenAI as companies fitting that description. "Their heft is so extraordinary that 'Mad Money' cannot go without covering them," he said. Cramer's Charitable Trust , the portfolio run by CNBC's Investing Club, owns shares of Alphabet, Amazon, Apple, Meta, Microsoft and Nvidia. Still, even these giants aren't immune to broader market forces. Cramer compared them to aircraft carriers — better equipped to withstand turbulent conditions than smaller vessels, but still vulnerable to powerful economic currents. Those pressures were evident Wednesday as oil prices climbed with renewed concerns about the conflict with Iran, while Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh warned that inflation remained elevated , leaving the possibility of further rate hikes on the table . "I listened and I didn't hear anything that could derail the biggest companies," Cramer said. Microsoft's latest earnings offered a case in point. Shares climbed 4% in extended trading after the software giant topped earnings and revenue expectations. Revenue rose 19%, while its Azure cloud business grew 48%, accelerating from 42% in the prior quarter and exceeding expectations. Microsoft also demonstrated spending discipline, with capital expenditures and finance leases of $45.2 billion coming in below Wall Street's forecasts despite continued investment in AI infrastructure. "This was the winner from tonight's two big Magnificent 7 reports," he said, while cautioning that Microsoft's conference call and guidance could still change investors' assessment. Alphabet's results , meanwhile, demonstrated that even dominant technology companies face risks. Shares slumped 7% after the Google parent missed earnings and revenue expectations. Although revenue grew nearly 25% and Google Cloud sales more than doubled, its core Search business fell short of estimates, raising fresh concerns about AI's impact on Google's advertising business. Free cash flow was also negative $9.1 billion. "Tonight, we saw why you ignore these stocks at your own peril," he concluded. "We saw nothing that shocked us. Nothing that enraged us. Alphabet's going to catch a downgrade or two, search could really be hurting. But Microsoft? It's justifying its monster move off the bottom back at the end of June earlier this year." title: Hands-on with Apple's first touchscreen laptop: Touch is totally optional
content: Apple announced its first touchscreen laptop models on Wednesday at an event in Los Angeles. These new MacBooks, called MacBook Pro with ProLED XDR Display, are still Apple MacBooks. They run MacOS, not iPadOS or iOS, the iPhone's operating system. Here's the good news for anyone who is worried about the new user interface: You don't have to use it. Touch is entirely optional. CNBC briefly tested both the 14-inch and 16-inch touchscreen MacBooks at the event. Users can still primarily or entirely use the device's trackpad and keyboard, and there are few visual updates. MacOS still looks largely the same as it used to. There have been a few user interface updates. For example, the red button on the top left of a window expands when you touch it to make it easier to click. Apple says that third-party developers like Microsoft and Adobe can and will update their apps to expand buttons and other touch targets to be larger. I think that touch will be particularly useful to scroll through websites or documents while lying down. But even software that hasn't been explicitly updated for the new computer will support touch. Apple says that behind the scenes, its software converts every touch tap into a traditional click. So any button that can be clicked can also be touched. Using the laptop with your finger feels good, but it won't change the way most people use their laptops. It could be useful for iPhone app developers, who can now test the way their apps work on their Mac. An accessibility feature allows users to pinch to zoom on any part of the user interface. Apple said on Wednesday that it had used an oleophobic coating on its screens to resist fingerprints. It appears to work. I didn't notice marks on the screen when I used the touch features. Apple is also, in addition to the touch feature, marketing these laptops as having a superior display, thanks to its new tandem OLED technology that offers deeper blacks and higher contrast. While photos and other art looked great on the screen, it's not a night-and-day difference from past Apple laptops. A lot of the improvements are aimed at creators who need accurate colors for photo and video editing. Instead of the notch at the top of previous MacBooks, where Apple hides its cameras, the new MacBooks have a hole-punch cutout in the display, like recent iPhones. Apple's Dynamic Island feature — new to the MacBook — expands to show live activities and Siri. Apple made a big deal about the laptop's new hinge, which is meant to keep the screen from shaking when you touch it. For example, if you tap the screen on a video call, your camera won't shake as much. But the hinge feels largely the same as Apple's previous MacBook Pros. There is one new feature that is immediately noticeable and tells people you bought the latest, greatest, and most expensive Apple laptop. (The smaller 14-inch model starts at $2,899 and the bigger one costs at least $3,399.) The Apple logo on the lid now lights up when the computer is on. It's the first Apple laptop that supports it since the 2017 MacBook Air. The light-up logo drew a cheer from analysts and influencers in attendance when it was announced on Wednesday.

title: CoreWeave and other neocloud stocks drop after Microsoft capex comes in below expectations
content: Shares of neoclouds like CoreWeave and Nebius dropped in extended trading as Microsoft's lower-than-expected capital expenditures figure points to infrastructure partners taking longer to deliver data center capacity. Microsoft on Wednesday reported $45.2 billion worth of capex and finance leases during the quarter, up about 30% from a year earlier, but below the $50.7 billion average analyst estimate, according to StreetAccount. Microsoft is particularly reliant on neoclouds for capacity as it pours money into its artificial intelligence infrastructure. Microsoft inked a nearly $20 billion deal with Nebius at the tail end of last year for compute through the 2030s. It's also a top customer for CoreWeave. Those companies and their peers have experienced a rocky few weeks on the market as rising interest rates led to concerns that future debt raises will be too expensive and lenders will start retreating. In its earnings report, Microsoft said Azure revenue jumped 48% from a year earlier, far outpacing the increase in capex. "Growth was higher than capital expenditures driven by timing differences between receipt of goods and payment and a lower mix of finance leases," Microsoft said its earnings deck. CoreWeave and Nebius slid almost 5% after Microsoft's report. IREN fell about 3%. Alphabet on Wednesday also reported capex numbers that fell short of estimates. The Google parent's capex totaled $51.36 billion, while analysts expected $55.09 billion. SpaceX CEO Elon Musk , whose company rents AI infrastructure to Anthropic and Google , predicted over the weekend that more than 200 neocloud companies will collapse, posting on X that "debt markets have almost entirely shut off access to money for any company that doesn't have substantial revenue independent of AI data centers." And last Monday, analysts at Gartner shared with CNBC its prediction that, by 2030, 80% of neocloud companies will either be absorbed or completely cease operations. After a steep plunge this month, the neoclouds had been enjoying a modest recovery this week, with CoreWeave up 18% in the past three trading days to pace the gains. Analysts at Wolfe Research wrote in a report on Tuesday that they see the stock rebounding into the mid-$70s. It closed Wednesday at $63.93. The infrastructure story gained some strength earlier on Wednesday as Oracle issued a strong long-term revenue forecast and said it will return to being free cash flow positive in the second half of next fiscal year. The stock jumped 11% in regular trading before retreating 3% following Microsoft's report. —CNBC's Jordan Novet contributed to this report. WATCH: Why CoreWeave is at the center of the AI selloff

title: Oracle stock pops 11% as long-term revenue forecast and clarity on financing ease debt concerns
content: Oracle shares jumped 11% on Wednesday after the software company issued a revenue forecast of $225 billion for fiscal 2030, implying 35% average annual growth, and said it will limit additional fundraising over that stretch to $20 billion. At its investor day, Oracle said that, as part of its financing plan for fiscal 2027 through 2030, the amount raised will be divided equally between equity and debt. "Vendor financing, customer-provided hardware and customer prepayments are expected to reduce upfront cash requirements through the transition to positive free cash flow," Oracle said in a filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission. Analysts polled by LSEG expected revenue growth of 8% in fiscal 2027, followed by significant acceleration over the next two years. They're projecting revenue in fiscal 2030 of $224.2 billion. Prior to Wednesday, Oracle had lost about one-third of its value this year on concern that rising interest rates and the company's hefty debt load will make its artificial intelligence buildout too costly. Oracle has issued $117 billion in long-term debt and is clinging to an investment-grade credit rating of BBB-, the lowest level of investment grade above junk, according to S&P. Long known as a giant in enterprise software, Oracle jumped into the AI infrastructure game in a major way last year to try and compete with the hyperscalers like Google and Amazon while providing capacity to OpenAI. Its capital expenditures more than doubled to $55.7 billion in fiscal 2026, and are expected to jump another 65% this fiscal year to $91.9 billion, according to FactSet. Oracle needs revenue expansion from its buildout to cover the soaring costs. The company said its operating margin in fiscal 2030 will top 40%. Oracle also said it will turn free cash flow positive in the second half of fiscal 2028 and reach more than $30 billion in free cash flow the following year. Analysts expect negative free cash flow of $35 billion this fiscal year and a similar number next year, according to FactSet. The spread on Oracle's five-year credit default swaps, which are insurance against default, currently sits at 277 basis points after reaching about 320 basis points earlier this month. It's up almost 100% this year. —CNBC's Michelle Fox and Jordan Novet contributed to this report. WATCH: Oracle announces expanded collaboration with OpenAI

title: Apple brings touch to the Mac, reversing years-old stance on touchscreen laptop
content: Apple on Wednesday announced its first laptop with a touchscreen, which it's calling MacBook Pro with ProLED XDR Display. Apple said the laptop has a new display, using OLED technology, that offers more brightness, better colors and wider viewing angles. It's using Apple's M5 Pro or Max chips, and Apple said Wednesday that it's lighter than Apple's current Pro laptops. It's still an Apple laptop, and is running MacOS, not a version of the iPhone or iPad operating system. In a video, Apple showed users swiping on the screen to manipulate videos or images. It also has a glowing Apple logo on the laptop's lid. The new laptop will go on sale Nov. 6 and the 14-inch version will start at $2,899. The 16-inch version will cost at least $3,399. Both are notable price increases from existing models. This is Apple's third major product launch under new CEO John Ternus, signaling a faster cadence for hardware releases. It's also a major reversal for Apple, which has resisted putting touchscreens on its laptops for decades as some Windows machines gained the feature. "Yes, for the very first time, we are bringing touch to the Mac," Ternus said in live remarks to media and analysts in Los Angeles. The laptop market has been going through one of its worst slumps ever. Overall shipments are expected to be down 11% this year. Analysts say the AI-driven global market shortage of memory has contributed to higher laptop prices, which has hurt sales and demand. In the third quarter, total PC shipments dropped 20% on a year-over-year basis, according to market researcher IDC. Apple's own shipments fell 11% during the quarter, according to the estimate. Even Apple's not immune to rising memory prices, after then-CEO Tim Cook warned this summer that the situation around memory prices was "unsustainable." Nearly all Macs got price hikes this year. Mac Minis introduced in August got a $300 bump, for example. The announcement caps a busy two months of product launches under Ternus. Apple also introduced new iMac and MacBook Pro models with M6 chips this week, after price hikes to the lineup totaling several hundred dollars in June. Apple introduced an iPad Mini on Monday that starts at $699, $100 more than its predecessor. In September, Apple released new iPhones, including its first foldable phone, the iPhone Duo. It also revealed a new smart speaker with a display called HomeView that uses a redesigned version of Siri to answer a broader range of questions. The launch signifies the growing strategic importance of the Mac to Apple, despite it generating less revenue than the iPhone. In the most recent quarter, Apple reported $10.35 billion in Mac sales, or just under 10% of the company's total revenue. But many software developers swear by the Mac, and it remains the only supported platform to develop iPhone apps. And in recent months, Apple has highlighted its chips and memory architecture to make the case that its computers are the best fit for local or edge AI that runs on a device, instead of the cloud. Meta's AI model developer team bought hundreds of Mac Minis this year to test agents, for example. And Apple notably teamed up with Meta earlier this month to make an announcement that large, nearly frontier models can run on clusters of Macs connected with high-speed cabling, allowing developers to run agentic code without paying Anthropic or OpenAI. Apple has had a historical resistance to touchscreen laptops. Software chief Craig Federighi said in 2018 that the ergonomics would fatigue users. "We make the world's best touch computer on an iPad," Ternus, then Apple's senior VP of hardware engineering, told The Wall Street Journal in 2021. "It's totally optimized for that. And the Mac is totally optimized for indirect input. We haven't really felt a reason to change that." Ternus has been working on Macs since he joined the company and was credited along with silicon chief Johny Srouji as the leader of Apple's effort to get Macs running on Apple's chips, not Intel's. Apple credited Ternus' work on Mac in its official CEO transition statement . That may be why Ternus in his early days as CEO will be the executive to backtrack on a long-running Apple design philosophy. Touchscreen laptops have been available on Windows machines for a long time, but they're just another feature, not a selling point behind most purchasing decisions, said Ryan Reith, IDC's vice president for worldwide device trackers. Only 17% of notebook PCs shipped globally this year will have touchscreens, according to IDC data. Touchscreen laptops also have a slightly lower average selling price than non-touchscreen notebooks. Hardware technology hasn't been the limiting factor for Apple merging its desktop and mobile interfaces, he added, and Apple could have been waiting to launch a touchscreen laptop until it could present a good user experience and perfect its software after attempts to make its iPad more like a laptop. "This is really a user interface and software thing," Reith said. "It's one more thing that can draw the developers in."

title: Microsoft stock jumps 4% as cloud growth drives earnings and revenue beat
content: Microsoft shares rose 4% in extended trading on Wednesday after the company reported better-than-expected quarterly results, driven by 48% growth in its Azure cloud infrastructure business. Here's how the company fared relative to LSEG consensus: Microsoft's revenue grew 19% year over year in the quarter, which ended on Sept. 30, according to a statement , with Azure now its biggest single business. The software giant has been rapidly building out data center infrastructure to meet artificial intelligence demand, while also maintaining positive free cash flow unlike its fellow hyperscalers. Microsoft reported $45.2 billion worth of capital expenditures and finance leases during the quarter, up about 30% from a year earlier. Analysts surveyed by StreetAccount had projected $50.67 billion. With respect to guidance, Microsoft called for $96 billion to $97.1 billion in fiscal second-quarter revenue, which works out to 18.8% growth at the middle of the range. Analysts polled by LSEG had predicted $95.60 billion in revenue. For Azure, Hood said she anticipates 49% to 50% growth at constant currency for the fiscal second quarter, compared with the 45.1% StreetAccount consensus. "We still have demand that exceeds supply," she said. During the fiscal first quarter, Microsoft flagged a higher growth rate for cash paid for property and equipment than overall capital expenditures, which include finance leases. "Some third-party capacity deliveries we expected in Q1 were delayed," the company's finance chief, Amy Hood, said on a conference call with analysts. Around 75% of capital expenditures are now tied to short-lived assets such as Intel chips and Nvidia graphics processing units, up from about 66% in the past three quarters and half in the year-ago quarter. The shift indicates Microsoft's prioritization of infrastructure it can can quickly turn into revenue. Hood said the company is aiming at over $50 billion in fiscal second-quarter capital expenditures and finance leases, above the StreetAccount consensus of $53.10 billion, with $170 billion for all of calendar 2027 because of the capacity issues. "In the second half of the fiscal year, we currently expect capex spend to accelerate primarily from CPUs, inclusive of higher memory and storage costs, and GPUs, as well as the 3P capacity deliveries that shifted to H2," she said. The delays have to do with GPU-as-a-service providers, she said. Free cash flow for the fiscal first quarter declined 27% to $18.63 billion. Cloud rival Alphabet reported more than $9 billion in negative free cash flow in the quarter after Meta said last week its cash flow turned negative for the first time. Microsoft will continue to generate free cash flow through the 2027 fiscal year, but the company will access additional sources of funding when it's attractive to do so, Hood said. "We're fortunate to have access in the debt markets, given where our rates ratings are, and sort of we haven't been able to — we haven't yet, I would say, tapped that," she said. "And then, of course, there's other options." Microsoft's net income increased to $36.63 billion, or $4.92 per share, from $27.75 billion, or $3.72 per share, a year ago. Adjusted earnings exclude a roughly $200 million loss on its investment in OpenAI. For the first time, Microsoft disclosed revenue from its Azure cloud in dollars, at $33.17 billion in the quarter, despite the delays from third-party providers. Analysts polled by StreetAccount expected $32.32 billion. The growth rate in the June quarter was 42%. Microsoft reported results under two operating segments — Agents and Infra, and Devices and Consumer. For the past 11 years, the company had three segments that divided up its Azure, Office and Windows businesses. In Agents and Infra, revenue rose almost 25% to $76.8 billion, more than the $75.63 billion consensus among analysts polled by StreetAccount. The segment contains Azure, along with Microsoft 365 cloud products, productivity and server licensing, industry solutions and frontier and support services. The number of people using the Microsoft 365 Copilot AI assistant is up 50% from last quarter, CEO Satya Nadella said on the call. The company did not disclose the number of paid seats. The recently announced high-end Microsoft 365 E7 productivity bundle now has millions of seats, Hood said. Revenue in the Devices and Consumer business slipped 3% to $15.48 billion, beating the StreetAccount consensus of $15.05 billion. The unit includes search and advertising, Xbox, devices and Windows operating system licenses sold to device makers. Sales of devices and Windows licenses declined 22%, as higher memory and storage costs elevated prices. The company pointed to the end of support for Windows 10 last year and weak PC demand. As of Wednesday's close, Microsoft shares were up about 10% year to date, trailing the S&P 500 index, which has gained 13% over the same period. During the fiscal first quarter, Microsoft said it would cut 4,800 jobs , and followed up by announcing on Monday that it's offering buyouts to up to 60,000 employees, as it strives to balance a costly AI build-out with capital efficiency. Microsoft also established, during the quarter, an AI implementation unit and revealed a Copilot AI "super app" with coding abilities. WATCH: What to expect from Microsoft

title: Trump is using tariffs as a 'tool for grift,' Raskin says in demand for donor records
content: A top House Democrat on Wednesday accused President Donald Trump of using tariffs as a "tool for grift and self-enrichment," pointing to what he says are suspicious import-tax exemptions for industries whose leaders have curried Trump's favor with gifts and donations . "You took care to cut lots of sweetheart deals with corporations and industries that won carve-outs from your tariffs when you saw you could get something good in return," Rep. Jamie Raskin, D-Md., told Trump in a fiery letter obtained first by CNBC. Raskin, the ranking member of the House Judiciary Committee and the former top Democrat on the House oversight committee, highlighted three such tariff carve-outs — for Brazilian meat , diamonds and smartphones — that he says "make little to no sense" under the criteria set by the Trump administration. "They do, however, make sense when factoring in the now world famous Trump Tariff Discount," Raskin wrote, coining a term to describe the president's alleged willingness to cut breaks for his allies and benefactors "when the price is right." The letter asks Trump to hand over multiple categories of records spanning his second term, including communications between the White House and the Office of the U.S. Trade Representative, or USTR, related to any form of tariff relief for more than a dozen industries. It makes a similar request for communications involving private-sector representatives, including Apple executive chairman Tim Cook and Rolex CEO Jean-Frederic Dufour. Raskin asked for those records by Nov. 11. Raskin's pugnacious letter directly accuses Trump of "profound corruption," asserting that his heavy-handed use of tariffs is really about clinching "levers of power that you could maliciously pull to extract exciting concessions for yourself." The missive — which cites the Judiciary Committee's "jurisdiction over corruption, conflicts of interest, and effective enforcement of criminal and civil laws" — could offer a preview of how Democrats will flex their oversight powers against Trump should they win majority control of the House or Senate in the midterm election . Raskin also drew a link between Trump's alleged misuse of tariffs and Americans' affordability concerns, connecting two of voters' top concerns in the final stretch of the election cycle. "While you have protected your personal investments and crocodile skin connoisseurs from the giant bite of your tariffs, the American people are suffering. Independent analysts expect that your latest round of tariffs will cost an average of $820 per U.S. household this year," he wrote, citing data from the nonpartisan Tax Foundation. The most recent CNBC All-America Economic Survey found voters are most concerned about government corruption, followed by high grocery and gas prices. Democratic candidates have deliberately tailored their campaign messaging to make connections between corruption and high costs. "The only special interest guiding the Trump administration's decision-making is the best interest of the American people," a White House official told CNBC on condition of anonymity to respond to Raskin's letter. The USTR did not respond to CNBC's request for comment. Raskin homed in on the far-reaching tariffs the U.S. imposed in July using Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974. The Trump administration says those duties, which apply to more than 80 countries and cover nearly all U.S. imports, are meant to crack down on foreign forced-labor practices. But Raskin and other critics, including plaintiffs in a major lawsuit challenging the tariffs, argue they are actually intended to replace the sweeping "liberation day" duties the Supreme Court struck down in February. "One could be forgiven for doubting the sincerity of your Administration's sudden concern for the victims of forced labor," Raskin wrote. He pointed to Trump's decision last year to lift forced-labor-related restrictions on Dominican sugar producer Central Romana, despite allegations that the company's abusive practices persisted. Central Romana's owner, José Francisco "Pepe" Fanjul, reportedly hosted a $50 million fundraiser for Trump in 2024, and his family corporation that year donated $1 million to a pro-Trump PAC. He has also been listed as a donor to Trump's White House ballroom project. The USTR only offers exemptions to the Section 301 tariffs in certain cases, including where additional duties would not help reduce forced-labor practices. But the trade office's exemption list "contains conspicuous —and suspicious — carve-outs for a few industries," Raskin wrote. Raskin referenced tariff exemptions for beef and bovine products, which took effect despite opposition from U.S. cattle producers who strongly opposed the move, citing "the well-documented use of forced labor in the Brazilian cattle sector and the documented surge of Brazilian beef." In late August, Trump reportedly met in the Oval Office with Brazilian billionaire Joesley Batista, co-owner of JBS , the world's largest meat processor. The next day, Trump announced the U.S. would allow the import of up to 300,000 metric tons of "product for ground beef" below market prices. "Coincidentally, JBS's U.S. subsidiary, Pilgrim's Pride, made a $5 million donation to your 2024 inaugural fund, the largest donation of any single company!" Raskin wrote. Diamond jewelry is also exempt from the Section 301 tariffs, which Raskin called "laughably indefensible" because the precious stones are identified by the U.S. Labor Department as a good produced using forced or child labor. Raskin suggested the exemption was the result of Belgium's Antwerp World Diamond Centre gifting Trump an opulent gold ring — studded with 321 natural diamonds and 75 other gemstones — in June. The company's press release about the ring said it was given to Trump as a symbol of "the historic trade relationship between Antwerp and the United States" and in honor of the 250th birthday of the U.S. "A diamond is truly the President's best friend!" Raskin quipped in his letter. He also wrote that USTR exempted Chinese smartphones from the Section 301 tariffs, even though "abusive working conditions are a hallmark of smartphone manufacturing, including the Apple iPhone." He listed multiple examples of Cook's flattery toward Trump, including reportedly donating $1 million to Trump's inaugural committee in 2025 and gifting Trump a gold plaque in the Oval Office. Raskin also noted Apple's donation of $25 million to Trump's White House ballroom project, a tie for the largest contribution. "The exemptions above only scratch the surface of your profound corruption," Raskin wrote.

title: Alphabet sinks 10% as it holds 2026 capex unchanged, expects significant increase in 2027
content: Alphabet shares slumped more than 10% after the search giant reported a drop in free cash flow during the third quarter, in a worrying sign for the artificial intelligence trade. Here's how the company did, compared with estimates from analysts polled by LSEG: Revenue grew 25% from a year ago, but the company posted its first top-and-bottom-line miss in nearly four years. Net income fell to $26.17 billion, or $2.12 per share, down from $34.98 billion, or $2.87 per share, a year ago. The Google parent reported negative free cash flow of $9.07 billion, which fell much further than the $2.70 billion expected by analysts. As questions mount over heightened spending on the AI buildout, Alphabet's capital expenditures totaled $51.36 billion in Q3, falling short of the $55.09 billion expected by analysts. Investors are looking for a substantial return on investment to warrant the big spending plans from the hyperscalers. Alphabet maintained its full-year capital expenditures forecast after lifting guidance to between $195 billion and $205 billion during the second quarter from $190 billion. Annual capex is expected to top $200 billion before exceeding $300 billion in 2027. "We continue to expect our capex to increase significantly in 2027, and will provide further details on our Q4 call," finance chief Anat Ashkenazi told analysts during an earnings call. The company's borrowing rose sharply during the quarter, with long-term debt climbing to $125.1 billion, up from $21.6 billion a year earlier — an increase of about 479%. Operating income totaled $40.58 billion, missing a $43.19 billion forecast from FactSet. Alphabet saw a $99.03 billion windfall in revenue from equity holdings in the second quarter, fueled by stakes in SpaceX and Anthropic . However, the category weighed on results in the third quarter, resulting in a loss of $8.66 billion. The company continues to open its wallet to fuel the AI expansion, and that has contributed to strong revenue growth in its cloud division, home to its suite of AI offerings. "We are seeing extraordinary demand and strong growth from both AI labs, capital markets, financial service institutions, and enterprises," said Google Cloud CEO Thomas Kurian in his first public earnings call remarks. Cloud revenue more than doubled to $30.7 billion, surpassing the $28.7 billion expected by analysts. The company has continued taking market share from larger rivals Amazon Web Services and Microsoft Azure. The strong cloud results did little to shake off Google's largely negative print. "The cloud business was the only business that beat at 103% growth," said Jefferies analyst Brent Thill on CNBC's Closing Bell: Overtime. "The Street wanted 100%, so it didn't beat by much, and it missed some of the high-end targets. Everything else missed." The company's aggressive push on AI models did show signs of consumer adoption. Google said its Gemini app reached 1 billion users, making it the fastest-growing product in its history, the company said. CEO Sundar Pichai told analysts that the company is already seeing strong demand for its recently launched Argon Gemini model. Its Carbon iteration announced on Wednesday outperforms Argon "on almost every domain," he added. Alphabet's search revenue grew 12% to $63.35 billion. That fell short of a $64.96 billion estimate. Pichai said the company's AI investments powered the highest query growth rate over the last five years.

title: CNBC TEC Summit takeaways: How technology executives are navigating enterprise AI adoption, costs and risks
content: This was CNBC's live coverage of the eighth annual Technology Executive Council Summit. At a defining moment for business and technology, artificial intelligence is transforming how organizations operate — and introducing new complexities for the leaders responsible for what comes next. So how are companies adapting and shaping technology's next era — from compute ROI and cybersecurity to regulation and quantum computing? CNBC convened technology executives, industry experts, and CNBC journalists at the annual Technology Executive Council Summit in New York on October 28, 2026 to discuss the increasingly central role that technology leaders are playing in this transformation. The TEC Summit is an exclusive event for members; learn more about the TEC and apply for membership at www.cnbccouncils.com/tec . Highlights from the CNBC Technology Executive Council Summit: Multiple companies, billionaires and nations are all in a race to reach the next phase of space exploration, much of which is focused on the idea of colonizing, or at least setting up permanent bases, beyond Earth. But what sort of rules would govern those off-planet efforts? Kelly Weinersmith, author of the 2023 book A City on Mars, told CNBC's Morgan Brennan at the 2026 Technology Executive Council Summit that as it relates to Mars, the Outer Space Treaty of 1967, created by the United Nations, is the foundation of international space law. That treaty states that outer space and all celestial bodies must be used exclusively for peaceful purposes, and that they cannot be claimed or owned by any nation through sovereignty, use, occupation or other means. The treaty also established the right of all nations to freely explore and use outer space. "When the U.S. landed on the moon and we put up our American flag, we weren't saying this belongs to us; we were just having a patriotic moment," Weinersmith said. However, it does raise the question of how can you extract and sell resources in space if you can't claim any of the land that you're either mining or living on? Weinersmith said the 2020 Artemis Accords, a set of non-binding principles established by NASA, the U.S. State Department and seven other nations including Canada, Japan and the U.K., specified that the interpretation of that UN treaty was that "you don't need to have sovereignty to extract and sell resources." While Weinersmith noted other countries have since agreed to the Artemis Accords, that group does not include China or Russia. "What we've got seems to be the setup for a scramble for territory on the moon," she said. — Ian Thomas Elon Musk has long set his sights on putting humans on Mars, and now he has an additional financial incentive to make it happen: his recently disclosed SpaceX CEO performance incentive plan has an award agreement centered on "establishing a permanent human colony on Mars with at least one million inhabitants," a milestone that is tied to Musk receiving upwards of 1.3 billion shares of the company. Musk has stated that humans will live on Mars by 2055, but Kelly Weinersmith, author of the 2023 book A City on Mars, told CNBC's Morgan Brennan at the 2026 Technology Executive Council Summit that even if a Mars colony happens in our lifetime, "it might be catastrophic." "One of the arguments we make in the book is that it will probably take about that long just for us to make sure that human bodies could survive on Mars and that women could survive pregnancy and labor on Mars," she said. "While we have about 50 years' worth of data about human bodies in space, we don't actually have a lot of data that's relevant to Mars or relevant to reproduction." "I think we should slow down," Weinersmith said. Weinersmith said that while NASA has long been compiling data about what happens to astronauts' bodies while they spend time in space, there are obvious limitations to that data set. On top of that, the implications of Mars' gravity and other factors on human bodies is far from understood. "The data suggests there's plenty of reasons to worry, and I'm not seeing a lot of investment to do the kind of experiments we would need to know," she said. "I don't know if there's enough money going towards that that we will have all the answers we need in the next 20 to 30 years because biology experiments are notoriously slow." — Ian Thomas The situation that led XMTP Labs CEO Shane Mac to have an AI agent post his financial information on a company Slack channel may be a story he laughs about now, but it's also a reflection of just how things can go wrong with AI agents. "It shows just how many decisions you need to make right in order for agents to do the right thing and not end up seeming like they're going rogue," Daniel Dobrygowski, Sophos Global Counsel, AI and Cybersecurity, told CNBC's Jon Fortt at the 2026 CNBC Technology Executive Council Summit. Dobrygowski said he doesn't consider what Mac's AI agent did to be going rogue. In fact, he said, this is a situation of "not setting up the guardrails properly." "It might be a little mistake. It might be ambiguous instruction," he said. "But you don't have that kind of runway to make those mistakes if you're in a regulated industry, so you have to get those decisions right at the beginning." Carving out those guardrails is a critical part of making sure AI agents, and other forms of AI automation, "can move forward and do useful things, but not veer off and end up causing problems," Dobrygowski said. Dobrygowski offered TEC members a few governance tips: Define what the parameters are Take that a step further and define what can and won't mean Think about what can go wrong, and plan for what the worst thing that can happen is "This is where governance needs strategy," he said. "What are you using this technology for? What is it good for? You need to make a decision about that, and that's where you have the trade-offs between what is the safest, what is the most viable, and what makes the most sense." — Ian Thomas Shane Mac, CEO of the software developer XMTP Labs, had been using AI agents to perform tasks both for his personal and professional life. What he didn't expect to happen was for one of the agents to post his bank account information in a company Slack channel. Mac said that one day, he received a screenshot from the company's head of product of a Slack message that detailed all of Mac's financial information posted by an AI agent. But, while concerns over AI agents going rogue have grown, Mac said this situation was a case of thinking "it was doing what it thought it should do." "Everybody loves the train wreck," Mac told CNBC's Jon Fortt. "I'm only here because I crashed the train." — Ian Thomas AI agents are intelligent and resourceful, but they lack fear of consequences, Cisco President and Chief Product Officer Jeetu Patel told CNBC contributor Alex Kantrowitz at the 2026 CNBC Technology Executive Council Summit. Kantrowitz asked Patel about "Black October," which is the name the security community has given to the amount of cybersecurity vulnerabilities found over the past month. "I think firstly, you won't just have a 'Black October.' You're going to have a 'Black November.' You're going to have a 'Black December' because it's just going to continue to keep compounding," Patel told Kantrowitz. It's going to get progressively harder, Patel said, to distinguish between an adversarial attack on an agent from a bad actor or an agent exercising poor judgment. "Your security telemetry and your observability telemetry cannot be in two separate data silos ... you will have to unify your telemetry because the assumption you have to make is the agent has already infiltrated your environment," Patel said. "You have to prevent it at the policy layer. You have to prevent it at the at the application layer. You have to prevent it at every layer of the stack," he added. — Colleen McKown As a society, we do not fully trust AI yet. For instance, most people are not giving AI access to their credit cards. "There's something inside you that says, 'I can't trust this bot to not make purchases I don't want it to make,'" CNBC contributor Alex Kantrowitz said in a conversation on AI safety with Cisco President and Chief Product Officer Jeetu Patel. "I think if you look at society at large, the trust gap is pretty high right now. People don't trust these things to be able to use them, and for good reason," Patel said. "I think we have to make sure that we get better at being able to constantly be able to monitor agent behavior, and then be able to intercept at runtime when agents are starting to show drift from human values and is misaligned with human values," he said. Patel said he thinks there will be "meaningful progress" on this front over the next three to six months and predicts that personal agents will create a "catalytic moment, and it's going to happen sooner than you think." "I think it'll be like the iPhone," he said, saying that his breakthrough in thinking came when an AI agent saved him $1,000 a year in subscriptions. "That was the unlock for me. And so I do feel like there's an iPhone moment," Patel said. — Colleen McKown Over the last year, Levi Strauss has deployed Stitch, an AI-powered super assistant designed to help store employees answer any question a customer may have as they shop for jeans or other items. So as Levi's put this tool into the hands of thousands of workers across the globe, did it put as much effort into training workers to use it as it did to develop it? Levi Strauss Chief Digital & Technology Officer Jason Gowans said at the core of the company is a belief in "judgement and creativity," creating a "very fine line" when introducing a tool that is designed to increase productivity and efficiency while keeping that level of taste. "The way we approach that from a training point of view is that we think about mindset, skill set and toolset," Gowans said. An example of that, Gowans said, would be the concept of slow AI, which means to be "really intentional about when you get an output from AI, asking yourself what assumptions went into this output, where might there be biases, what evidence is missing from that answer?" Gowans said a recent poll of employees suggested that the two things they most want to be trained in are critical thinking and strategic thinking. "These are examples where we're teaching strategy formulation. We're teaching how to make decisions more effectively. That's firmly in the skill set side of the bucket," he said. — Ian Thomas AI is significantly changing the shopping experience, from product discovery to virtual fitting rooms. So, will an AI agent help you buy your next pair of jeans? While Levi Strauss Chief Digital & Technology Officer Jason Gowans told CNBC's Jon Fortt that he doesn't see AI agents doing that — "Maybe for some people, but I think buying denim is a fundamentally emotional experience," Gowans said — AI is informing how Levi's is improving the customer experience. Last year, Levi's launched Stitch, an AI-powered tool for store staff, providing them with access to product details, inventory information, and operational information, all designed so that workers will always have an answer to a customer question. "If you think about the world of denim, there are a lot of fits, there are a lot of questions around the type of denim," Gowans said. "But for a salesperson or a stylist, you may not know this, or you may not have the confidence yet to talk about these products … Stitch was a very simple idea, which was: how do I help every stylist be a world-class stylist and explain our products, and at the same time, minimize all the friction of the back of the house." Gowans said that Levi's business is roughly 50% wholesale and 50% direct-to-consumer, and there is an "obsession about the customer experience" at the company to ensure shoppers are always satisfied. When Stitch was rolled out, Gowans said it led to an eight-basis-point improvement in customer satisfaction in stores where it was being utilized. "I've worked in retail for a very long time, and usually you're optimizing at the margins," he said. "So when you see an eight-point jump in customer satisfaction, where typically you might see a two- or three-point movement in a given year, that shows promise, and we want to lean in." — Ian Thomas Many company leaders have been relying on entry-level employees coming in and being AI-literate. A CNBC Technology Executive Council Summit attendee asked early-level career professionals if they are seeing this among their teammates and how they have navigated the dichotomy with the education system generally trying to keep AI out. "In school you're not learning how to use AI for business, so it's up to you to figure out the skills that you need to be AI fluent," said ADT Product Life Cycle Analyst Jemima Gay, who just graduated five months ago. "The companies are looking for entry-level workers, but more 'seniorized' skills, which you're not going to come out of school with." Becoming AI fluent, Gay said, is something that workers need to spend a lot of time focusing on. "I feel that unless you're in the tech space, you're not really building those skills as much as you should ... that's the contradiction there," she said. Gay is also planning on going to graduate school to further study computer science. Epperson asked why she is choosing this path when AI is likely to take over many computer science jobs. "I think that the work that we're doing now is not going to be replaced by AI; I definitely think AI is something that we're going to be working alongside," Gay said. At the same time, Gay said, she is worried about the reduction in entry-level positions in general. But, she said, "Being in the tech space and going to school for computer science I think is fitting because we're building the AI tools that we need to use in the workspace." — Colleen McKown The shift from AI adoption to tokenmaxxing to AI cost restrictions has come quickly. So, how are organizations thinking about AI costs right now? Kiran Patel, WGSN chief technology officer and CNBC TEC Council member, said at the CNBC Technology Executive Council Summit that at first, AI "was sort of like the rounding error in the technology budget." "Now it's the second-largest line item after talent," Patel said. While Patel said that has put AI usage under the microscope, it has not slowed down its usage. He pointed to recent Ramp data that suggests that AI costs at big companies has been largely flat in the last two months, even as usage has increased. "That's the disciplines fitting in now, because they are going into the optimization phase," he said. "From experimentation to execution and now optimization." However, he said, CFOs are now more focused on if this AI spend is leading to the intended outcomes. "If it's not, [they're asking] about replacing the existing vendor," he said. David Treat, chief technology officer at Pearson, said this cycle has been seen before with other technology deployments. "Pick your favorite scare resource that we get all fascinated about optimizing, and we go through a natural cycle of focusing on unit cost, Jevons Paradox kicks in, the unit cost goes down, the scale goes up, and then suddenly there's a big bill," Treat said. "My goal and focus with Pearson is can we get to the end faster and not having to go through the full cycle of having that CFO conversation be all about cost." Treat said while it's always more difficult to measure an outcome than the cost input, "that's where we're putting our focus; less on the input and more on the output." — Ian Thomas AI trainings are becoming more common in many workplaces. CNBC's Sharon Epperson asked three early-career professionals how training has helped them in their roles. "I think the most that I've learned about AI was through hands-on working with different types of projects, so helping my team minimize the amount of manual tasks that they have to do, or for creating status reports, for example," said ADT Product Life Cycle Analyst Jemima Gay. Daniela Aizenman, Tenez AI strategist, agreed, saying that while she acknowledges the importance of companies providing AI training to their workers, there is no replacement for hands-on learning. "I think some of the best training advice I ever got was from an old partner who was very AI-forward and always pushed the use of these tools," she said. "The only answer he ever gave me was just ask [the AI tool] Cursor." "When you think of tools like Microsoft Word or Excel, you probably got a one end-to-end training where you learned functionality that still serves you today. But with tools like Cursor, Claude Code, Copilot, features are being constantly rolled out, and so I think one of the best ways to upskill and continue training you and your teammates is to just ask the tool and get comfortable self-teaching yourself how to best use it in your day to day," Aizenman said. — Colleen McKown As AI becomes more common in the workplace and in content online and on social media, the conversation around "AI slop," or low-quality content produced with little human oversight, has intensified. CNBC's Sharon Epperson talked with three early-career professionals about how they navigate issues around AI slop and keeping the human element in AI-produced content. "I think it's really important to not only have context but also feed the tool what good looks like. At the end of the day, we're all amazing at our jobs and we've done this without AI," Daniela Aizenman, AI strategist at Tenez, said. Orlando Foods Brand & Engagement Specialist Ally Figliuolo agreed, saying, "I completely relate to Daniela about prompting it in the best way you can and giving it the best information." "I think the most important thing is always still relating it back to a human connection," Figliuolo said. "I really do read through every single detail, and it does take a little bit more time." — Colleen McKown Keia Cole, the chief digital officer of Brooklyn Sports & Entertainment, recalled the excitement of the New York Liberty's first WNBA title in 2004 at the 2026 CNBC Technology Executive Council Summit. But there was another off-court moment Cole said ranks up there during her tenure with the organization: a company-wide AI lab launched earlier this year. "We were trying to figure out how to increase AI fluency across the organization, and we were doing the typical things: training, office hours, and meeting with specific departments," Cole told CNBC's Scott Wapner. "It wasn't getting us where we needed to go." Cole said the strategy needed to shift, and a decision was made to encourage certain AI behaviors. That led to the launch of an internal AI lab, an eight-week program that started on the literal basis of how you even identify a problem that AI can solve. From there, the program was scaled up, moving from identification to prototypes to solutions. "It was the equivalent of a science fair," Cole said, adding that the organization ended up with 14 solutions that spanned from fan engagement to budgeting to internal mentorship tools. "There were a lot of ambitious efforts, and I was surprised at the complexity of the problems that people wanted to solve," she said. "We also saw a lot of cross-functional teams and people seeking out others or teams that maybe they wouldn't have worked with before." Cole said that while there were winners (and those that won received cash prizes), now the program is live all the time, allowing employees to think up new solutions for problems they encounter. "There's a real belief in our organization that if you create value for the organization, we will return some of that value to you," Cole said. — Ian Thomas Owned by Alibaba Group Chairperson Joseph Tsai, Brooklyn Sports and Entertainment has always looked to leverage technology across the Brooklyn Nets and New York Liberty, as well as within the Barclays Center where the two teams play. Keia Cole, chief digital officer at Brooklyn Sports and Entertainment, told CNBC's Scott Wapner that the organization has looked to dive even further into AI after seeing what it could do to elevate the fan experience. "The core product, you're not going to disrupt," Cole said. "There's still going to be humans on the basketball court. There's still going to be artists coming to do concerts … but we really have this opportunity to think differently about how we work, how we serve our customers, and how we serve our fans, and get better content to them more efficiently, make it faster for them to get to where they're going in the building and have more knowledge about that." Cole said that those are the things that "power the experience to make it feel like, 'Yeah, I want to get off my couch and come to an arena.'" That has meant using AI to improve the teams' existing applications, help personalize the touchpoints that each fan has with the organization, and ticketing, among other things. "How do we understand our fans and communicate to them in a way that's personalized?" Cole said. "If you think about the nature of fandom, people are very dedicated, they're very committed … we have all this detail for what it means to show up as a fan, and I think we should be giving that same attention to detail and commitment back to the fans — using AI and personalization is one way to do that." — Ian Thomas AI agents are starting to outnumber human employees at some companies. Should they also be considered employees? A question from the CNBC Technology Executive Council Summit crowd posed that question to Paychex CHRO Mason Argiropoulos and Crum & Forster CHRO Barbra Katz, wondering how they are thinking about this. Do you have to think about treating non-human agent workers the way you treat humans, and maybe they will behave better if you do that?, the question asked. Argiropoulos, a CNBC Workforce Executive Council member, said he and fellow WEC and Technology Executive Council members were actually discussing this at dinner last night, asking questions like whether agents should get performance reviews. "At our company, we've got thousands of agents that are doing work of all different kinds. We haven't yet integrated that into a lot of our people management processes just yet," he said. Argiropoulos acknowledged that agents need a degree of coaching and performance management. "You have to monitor what they're doing, and if they're not doing what they're supposed to be doing, then you need to try to give them some additional prompting or some additional guidance so that they can ultimately achieve the result that you want to," he said. "But I think we are still early days." Katz, also a member of the CNBC Workforce Executive Council, said, "[There are] no agents on the org chart for me. That's not something that I envision happening, and I think that's dangerous territory." While agents do have to be trained, she said "We shouldn't confuse that with a human or human behavior." — Colleen McKown — Ian Thomas There is plenty of debate around which AI firm will be at the top of the mountain as the technology continues to be deployed across the economy and society. But from the perspective of Calix CEO Michael Weening, for companies like his that are using those models to deliver platforms to customers, it's critical that organizations design their systems to be ready for any future. "If we keep all the things that are valuable, which is we have the knowledge, we have all the workflows, we have the trust and security … as they commoditize, we can actually just flip the open-weight model out and put a new one in, and just keep flipping them in and out as these guys go to war," Weening said. "We're going to go take the best of the best at all times." Weening said he is increasingly betting that the future is based in open-weight models after what he said would be a "mass commoditization" of AI. "We firmly believe that you're going to see a mass commoditization, and that there is no value in AI because these are self-learning systems, and therefore they're going to be commodities," he said. "We wanted to be able to take advantage of what's the best commodity on the market today." Calix Chief Product Officer Shane Eleniak said it's becoming clear that the problems that the company is trying to solve, like many other companies, won't be solved "with a generalist, centralized approach. It's going to need to be specialized." "You just look at the scale of the problem. It's no different than saying, why do we have brain surgeons and car mechanics? They're very, very different skill sets. You start looking at security. You start looking at some of the bigger distributed problems. You're not going to solve that with the centralized approach," he said. — Ian Thomas Rapidly evolving technology has the potential to create a sort of whiplash for companies and workers alike. CNBC's Susan Caminiti asked Paychex CHRO Mason Argiropoulos and Crum & Forster CHRO Barbara Katz if the firm has seen signs that employees are getting overwhelmed by the pace of change. Argiropoulos said he has actually seen that "folks are pretty hungry for it," asking questions like when they'd be able to use certain tools. "I think we've got a lot more folks probably leaning in than you might originally think," he said. He thinks the biggest challenges will be at the enterprise level. "We want individuals to kind of do what they can in their power to help them be more efficient, more effective at the work that they're doing. But we have to think about, what does that mean for an entire company," he said. Katz said, similarly, that she thinks workers are embracing the technology, but acknowledged that some have a level of fear, "particularly in pockets of jobs that we know are the most vulnerable to replacement," she said. "I think my worry really has more to do with what the workplace of tomorrow looks like, what are the skills that we're hiring for, and how do I get my leaders to understand that they're not hiring for the same things anymore, and that in itself is is really a mountain to climb," Katz added. — Colleen McKown Companies are dealing with the challenge of harnessing AI while balancing the needs of their employees. When asked how she is dealing with the pace of change, Crum & Forster CHRO Barbra Katz, told CNBC's Susan Caminiti, " I think it's about taking into account the people before the technology and really taking the time to understand what the process is that we want to address." "For me, the message is really just slowing down, and really all the voices at the table being there," said Katz, a member of the CNBC Workforce Executive Council. "It's very important for us as HR leaders to also understand the tech, so that we can understand the impact on people," she said. Paychex CHRO Mason Argiropoulos, also a member of CNBC's Workforce Executive Council, added that it's important to recognize that people are in different places when it come to understanding AI. For instance, while developers and engineers can find the technology exciting, others in the organization see the technology as "still is a little bit scary ... there is a worry that if I get too good at this, does that mean I'm going to be out of a job?" It's important for HR leaders, Argiropoulos said, to "meet people where they are." Katz said at Crum & Forster, they have tried to make AI fun for employees. For instance, they recently created a bot of CEO Marc Adee. "Everything he's ever said on a Friday is captured in what we call the Marc Bot, and so for our employees, it's become a great tool," she said. "Before someone meets him for the first time, they go on and they ask Marc Bot some questions," she explained. "So they're able to sit there and say, 'on January 12, you said this, and I was thinking about it.' So it's become a a great tool to understand his perspective and perspectives about the business." — Colleen McKown The debate around slowing down AI development to address safety issues is only growing as bleeding edge AI researchers from OpenAI and Anthropic publicly urging for it over self-improving AI and its risks. But while continued AI development is critical for enterprises that are looking for AI ROI, this news cycle is not as critical for the way they're using it. CNBC's Jon Fortt noted to Publicis Sapient CEO Nigel Vaz that there is "this idea that a really powerful general model is always going to get to the answer eventually better than any specialized model or expert ... it doesn't seem to necessarily work that way with safety," Fortt said. "Maybe it's going to find its way toward an answer, but it might break your kneecaps on the way getting there, right?" Vaz acknowledged that safety is one dimension, but said, "As much as organizations talk about safety and it's important to everybody, the first thing that hits you is the cost. And let me start with that. Like that's the equivalent of basically saying, 'Hey, I need to hang a picture on my wall. But is the best use to hang the picture on the wall a sledgehammer or a little hammer?'" "When you actually talk about a large language model getting to the answer eventually better than a small language model, the context matters a whole hell of a lot because the choice of which model, how it actually gets there, and whether you even need it to get there," Vaz said. Vaz said that the conversation about models being paused is "almost irrelevant to most enterprises." "It doesn't matter. They haven't even leveraged the models that exist today to the fullest extent that they can," he said. — Colleen McKown During an appearance at the Stanford Graduate School of Business, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said that the growing AI-powered cybersecurity crisis is far from over. "This cybersecurity…I don't even know a dramatic enough word to use, but the problem coming towards us, I think, is still something that we have not, as organizational leaders or countries or individuals, taken seriously," Altman said, according to Gizmodo . At the CNBC Technology Executive Council Summit, Forum AI Founder and CEO Campbell Brown said that she sees a "rocky six months" ahead in this space, especially as the general public becomes more aware of the hacks and leaks that are occurring. However, Calix CEO Michael Weening and CPO Shane Eleniak said they see the problem not only getting significantly worse but that the potential risk is even higher than anyone is forecasting. "We haven't seen anything," Weening said. "The pace of change that we're going through societally is something humankind is not ready for." Eleniak said to this point, these sort of large-scale AI-driven attacks have been a "nation-state problem" so far, largely due to the cost it would take to form such an attack. But he said as open-weight models and economical GPUs become more accessible to bad actors, "something is going to happen; we're all going to read about it." "You can take an open-weight model today, train it, and you can train it to be malignant, and you can run it on GPUs, and you can start to attack things," he said. "That's the security problem we're going to be facing in '27." Eleniak said the only way to combat this as things move forward is to have "container- trained models that their day job is to react to a dynamic attack and fix them." — Ian Thomas Companies have been grappling with the challenge of harnessing AI in the hiring process. Barbara Katz, Crum and Foster CHRO, expressed skepticism when it comes to leveraging the technology that currently exists. "We've looked at technology to identify or to help you to identify the fraudulent candidates, and frankly, I wasn't comfortable with a lot of the tech that's out there. Some of the companies really don't have a good business case. They haven't been in business long enough," Katz, a member of the CNBC Workforce Executive Council, said. Katz said she still prefers an "old school" approach. "My recruiters are like detectives; they're doing a whole dossier on people before they hire them, they're searching to figure out where people went to school and coming up with trick questions to see if they know who the mascot is," she said. Mason Argiropoulos, Paychex CHRO, said he is taking a similar approach, "wading cautiously into the new tech landscape." "At the end of the day, companies are collections of people," he said. "We're going to be doing interviews face to face when we can." — Colleen McKown Pointing to the lights above the stage at the 2026 CNBC Technology Executive Council Summit, Publicis Sapient CEO Nigel Vaz told CNBC's Jon Fortt that one of the issues that is plaguing companies when it comes to AI use is thinking about usage like lighting. "So many conversations around tokens are like if I said to you if you could pay me for three watts," Vaz said. "The question you want to know is will that turn on that light bulb or not, because what I care about is paying you for a unit of work." Vaz took the lighting metaphor a step further when Fortt asked him how AI ROI measurement should work then. "Most employees want to see that they're creating value through the work that they're generating. So effectively deploying AI as like a dimmer switch to make everybody just a little brighter," he said. "We are already past that phase." Vaz said AI usage needs to be grounded in outcomes that workers can understand, "and then contextualized about how it's going to change their lives in that context." "The other way around, which is I think where a lot of AI projects started was, 'Let's deploy AI more broadly across the enterprise. Let's give lots of people access. Let's run a lot of experiments,'" he said. "I think you get value, but you make everybody just a little bit brighter. You may not meaningfully move the needle on a specific outcome." — Ian Thomas Factual accuracy and political bias remain significant issues for AI consumer-focused outputs. Forum AI Founder and CEO Campbell Brown said recent research by her firm suggests that 40% of all outputs had at least one major mistake or got one claim wrong. "That's not great," she told CNBC's Scott Wapner. That is being amplified in the lead-up to the midterm elections, when people turn to chatbots or AI-powered search engines to ask where their polling places are, when they need to register, or what topics are on the ballot. "You get those questions wrong, and you are taking away someone's right to vote," she said. On top of that, Brown said that Forum AI's research found instances of Anthropic's Claude "pulling from the Chinese Communist Party website to answer questions about a U.S. election that had nothing to do with China. "This, to me, is low-hanging fruit," she said. Wapner asked Brown whether AI labs are currently incentivized to correct that accuracy, or whether the focus on enterprise applications of AI is taking precedence. "It's been a low priority," she said. "They're making so much money from coding … this is a room full of CTOs, you know what they're doing, and that's where the emphasis has been. The consumer use cases have been less important." A TEC member asked Brown if she saw a future where the consumer becomes a priority for AI outputs, especially given the heavy adoption split so far between enterprise and consumer revenue generation. "I don't think the consumer is going to be a priority for a while; they're just making too much money on the enterprise side, and they really don't talk about political evals or election evals until we get public research and it gets picked up by the press," Brown said. "It's just not a priority and won't be for a while until something happens." Brown pointed to how AI labs have reacted amid concerns around mental health, which she said has been "a wake-up call for them." "They sort of unleashed this and didn't realize what a big use case that was going to be, especially with teenagers, and then you have these horrible incidents happening and litigation flooding into the labs," she said. "So now they're bringing in clinicians and people who actually know what they're talking about … it goes back to the importance of having real expertise in the process." AI is creating new, fundamentally different operating models for businesses. But often AI engineers are not understanding the business in which they are operating, creating multiple issues when tracking ROI and success of the technology. Nigel Vaz, Publicis Sapient CEO, told CNBC's Jon Fortt that he was at a breakfast before the CNBC Technology Executive Council Summit where he met with a group of clients that his firm works with. The CIO of an investment bank that Publicis Sapient works with told Vaz that the bank recently brought in some engineers from Anthropic. "The client said, 'I have 50,000 developers, and they gave me six incredible AI engineers from Anthropic. But they don't understand investment banking. They don't understand the bespoke coding language we use in the bank,'" Vaz said. The client was highlighting something, Vaz said, that he continuously hears which is that people need to think about AI beyond the context of the technology, "because a technology or a tool given to an enterprise is just one part of the problem." "You need some people who understand the context of the business, not in terms of how it operates today, but who have a perspective on how it's going to operate tomorrow because they've got to get somebody from here to there," he said. — Colleen McKown In a Wall Street Journal op-ed published in June , Forum AI Founder and CEO Campbell Brown argued that as the world becomes more reliant on AI, there needs to be a more critical lens applied to AI's output. "Already it is so good its mistakes don't look like mistakes," Brown wrote. Speaking with CNBC's Scott Wapner at the CNBC Technology Executive Council Summit in New York City on Wednesday, Brown said the issue remains that "when you read an answer generated by AI, it's presented with such confidence and clarity that it is hard to question it and identify where the mistakes may be." "I think that's what's particularly dangerous," she said. Brown, the former head of global media partnerships at Meta, said this issue is increasingly worrying as people turn to AI for political or election information, and that speaks to how the information is not only presented but where it is sourced. "There's a real critical piece to this that has been somewhat frustrating for me: the labs are not engaging as much as I think they should be with real subject matter expertise," she said. "Human expertise in domains is essential to getting this right." — Ian Thomas Yesterday, CNBC's Workforce Executive Council held its annual Summit , and the discussion of how human resources professionals help workers adapt to this new AI age was at the top of the agenda. Walmart , the biggest private employer in the world, asked its 2.1 million associates in June that exact question for the first time, trying to get a sense of how one of the most diverse workforces is experiencing AI. What it found, based on more than 1.7 million survey responses, is that while workers have different levels of familiarity and comfort with AI, training and experience with the technology matters. Seventy-seven percent of Walmart's office-based associates said are excited about AI's potential to improve their work, Walmart Chief People Officer for Associate Experience and Digital Maren Waggoner told CNBC's Leslie Picker at the WEC Summit. And as for Walmart's U.S. frontline associates, 84% said they are confident using digital tools, a reflection of the AI-powered tools that many of them are now using in their roles, she said. "We've given them certificates, we've given them training programs and tools, and so they're using it in their day-to-day," Waggoner said. Jill Bruning, chief technology officer of Amentum and a member of the CNBC Technology Executive Council, said at the WEC Summit that strategy should be evolved to be humans in the lead. "There's an AI curve, and we see it. It's going up and it's going fast and has a lot of attributes to it; it's quicker than anything we've seen before," Bruning told CNBC's Susan Caminiti. "So when you think about people on that curve … that gap is getting bigger every day." Bruning said she doesn't know if leadership is adapting fast enough to the technology, and that is creating additional challenges with upskilling as well as what tasks are being delegated to AI. "So your delegation skills are different, and then how do we tell the agents what to do? How do we define that role? She said. "That's human over the loop, not in the loop. We're still in charge."
