Discussions will also center on AI regulation, agents, how workers are using the technology and where this acceleration of AI is taking society. Speakers include: — Ian Thomas

title: Google alters its cloud playbook, enlisting partners to sell more AI chips
content: Google has spent years pitching customers on the advantage of buying its chips, models and cloud services in one place, offering a full stack that rivals Amazon and Microsoft have tried to replicate. Now, the company is pushing its equipment outside of its own walls to reach more customers and build a bigger business around artificial intelligence chips, a market that Nvidia has dominated. A day ahead of its third-quarter earnings report, Alphabet said Tuesday that Oracle will offer Google's tensor processing units, or TPUs, the custom chips the internet giant has been developing since 2013 . It's the first time customers will be able to access TPUs outside of Google's infrastructure, and shows that cloud boss Thomas Kurian, who previously spent more than 20 years at Oracle, is looking elsewhere for growth. "They're a very strong competitor, and it's very possible that they could eventually take market share from Nvidia," said Chris Ballard, managing director of Check Capital Management, referring to Google's position in chips. Kurian, who joined Google in late 2018, is operating from a position of strength. Analysts expect Google Cloud revenue to jump about 90% from a year earlier, after growing 82% in the second quarter , with TPUs contributing to its momentum. "Google was great at doing its own thing, but it was never able to serve customers," said Uday Cheruvu, a portfolio manager at Harding Loevner, which owns Alphabet shares. "That mindset has changed." Google opened up TPUs to outside data centers in the second quarter, before this week's announcement with Oracle. Estimates for the TPU business vary widely, but they all point to significant growth. TD Cowen models $9.4 billion in TPU sales for the second half of this year and $62.5 billion for 2027. Wells Fargo expects about $9 billion in third-quarter sales and $99 billion next year. CFO Anat Ashkenazi said on the last earnings call in July that only a small portion of TPU revenue from existing agreements will be recognized this year, with the "vast majority" coming in 2027. She also said Google planned to use more outside capacity in the third quarter while the company builds out its own infrastructure. With $25 billion in second-quarter cloud revenue, Google trailed Amazon Web Services at $42 billion and Microsoft Azure at $29 billion. But Google is growing the fastest. "It's almost like the bigger the pie is getting, the faster they're accelerating into it," said Ballard, whose firm owned about $236 million in Alphabet stock as of June 30. While Kurian aims to get more TPUs into the market by turning to outside partners, he has to balance the benefits of building the customer base with his company's own technology needs. At a Goldman Sachs conference in September, Kurian said Google's AI servers pay for themselves in under two years, and servers running its own silicon reach payback in roughly half that time. "It's because we can optimize that whole stack," Kurian said. Industry research firm SemiAnalysis estimates that Google's latest Ironwood TPU costs about 44% less to own and operate than an Nvidia GB200 server. There's also the margin hit that comes with external TPU sales. TD Cowen estimates a 20% operating margin on TPU sales, compared with an overall cloud margin of about 35% last quarter. Cheruvu said he doesn't think Google's cloud operating margin could widen much beyond the mid-30s. Google declined comment. Google's biggest TPU customer is one of its top AI competitors. Anthropic, whose Claude models compete with Gemini, agreed last October to use up to 1 million TPUs in a deal worth tens of billions of dollars. Mizuho says that agreement brings nearly a gigawatt of capacity online this year and describes the relationship as Google "arming its closest model competitor." OpenAI is also planning to buy TPUs from Google, CNBC confirmed after The Information first reported on the ChatGPT maker's intentions on Tuesday. Anthropic is getting outside help to finance its Google silicon. This week, Broadcom , which works with Google on TPUs, detailed a $63 billion vehicle backed by Blackstone and three big banks that will buy TPUs and networking gear from Broadcom and lease them to Anthropic for five years. According to analysts from William Blair, the financing plan covers about half of Anthropic's 2027 needs, which suggests more financing is coming. In its initial public offering filing on Monday, Anthropic said it uses silicon from Google, Amazon, Nvidia and Advanced Micro Devices , allowing the company to "select chips based on the best price-performance and efficiency characteristics for each workload." Regarding Google and Broadcom, Anthropic said the partnerships "provide us with access to compute capacity powered by Google TPUs across multiple generations of the TPU platform." title: Stellantis stock rises 13% as automaker's turnaround plan, cost cuts gain traction
content: Shares of Stellantis were up Wednesday as the European car giant's third-quarter results showed it was making progress with its 60 billion euro turnaround plan. Third-quarter revenues rose 1% to 37.6 billion euros from a year ago, the Chrysler and Jeep owner said on Wednesday, while adjusted operating income rose 184% to 256 million euros from 90 million euros a year earlier. The automaker's industrial free cash flow improved to negative 4 billion euros, up from negative 4.3 billion the year prior. Stellantis on Wednesday also reconfirmed its 2026 guidance and target to achieve positive free cash flow next year, which is a main focus for investors. "Q3 was soft, but consensus expectations were far lower. Key here is that '26 Guidance was maintained while other auto OEMs and suppliers are cutting on elevated costs," RBC Capital Markets analyst Tom Narayan said Wednesday in an investor note. Stellantis stock on the New York Stock Exchange rose 13% on Wednesday to close at $4.69 a share. Shares in Milan closed at 4.28 euros, up 15.4%. Shares in both markets remain sharply down since the beginning of the year. Stellantis CEO Antonio Filosa told investors Wednesday that the company is ahead of schedule on its turnaround plan, which was announced in May. He said Stellantis expects to exceed its previously announced cost-cutting efforts of 6 billion euros under the plan by 2028, including 2.4 billion euros to start 2027. "We are very confident in reaffirming our '26 guidance. Those include '27 free cash flow positive," Filosa said Wednesday in response to concerns about the carmaker's ability to achieve its free cash flow target. Stellantis' 2026 guidance includes a mid-single-digit percentage increase in net revenue and a low-single-digit adjusted operating margin. Stellantis' turnaround plan includes investing 36 billion euros in its portfolio of automotive brands, with 60% of the cash to go towards its struggling North America sector. It also plans to introduce new vehicles, refresh models, and incorporate new technologies in its products. Stellantis is targeting roughly 23% revenue growth, from 154 billion euros last year to 190 billion euros by 2030, with a 7% adjusted operating margin by then. European carmakers, including Stellantis, have been struggling in China as domestic brands like Xiaomi, BYD and Geely gain ground and intensify competition. Just this week, German luxury carmaker Porsche said it would reduce its exposure to China as car sales decline in the region. Meanwhile, Mercedes-Benz said its third-quarter car sales slumped due to a "challenging market environment," in the country. Earlier this month, Filosa told CNBC that European regulators need to do more to incentivize carmakers to manufacture vehicles in the region to fend off Chinese rivals. Filosa called for regulation that "incentivizes, rewards, and protects the ones that are able to demonstrate that they design cars, engineer cars."

A nearly 20-year-old scientific prediction has gained experimental support, revealing how graphene’s atomic structure could unlock new possibilities for advanced sensors and electronic devices. A wrinkle in graphene just a few atoms wide can dramatically alter how electricity behaves in the material. Scientists have now measured this effect in exceptionally sharp folds, providing experimental evidence for a phenomenon predicted nearly 20 years ago. The discovery, published in Advanced Materials , suggests that researchers could eventually control electrical properties by changing a material’s shape rather than its chemical composition. Graphene, a remarkably strong and conductive material consisting of a single layer of carbon atoms, is already being explored for batteries, computer chips, and other advanced electronics. The effect is known as flexoelectricity, which occurs when uneven bending causes electrical charges to separate within a material. In graphene, extreme curvature can shift electrons toward one side of its atomically thin structure, creating an electric dipole with oppositely charged regions. The researchers examined naturally occurring wrinkles whose sharpest bends were compressed into spaces only a few atoms wide, less than a billionth of a meter (about 0.00000004 inches). They found that the sharpness of a wrinkle mattered far more than its overall height. Their estimates indicated that these highly curved regions produced electrical polarization between 100,000 and 10 million times stronger than that associated with much larger, gentler bends. “The sharpness of the wrinkle turned out to be much more important than its overall size,” said lead author Sathvik Ajay Iyengar, who earned his doctorate at Rice University and is now at the University of California, Berkeley. “That tells us we can potentially tune electrical behavior by carefully controlling curvature at the nanoscale.” The theoretical foundation for the discovery dates back nearly two decades. Vincent Meunier, now head of Engineering Science and Mechanics at Penn State, and Sergei V. Kalinin, now at the University of Tennessee, predicted in a Physical Review B paper that sharply bending graphene could rearrange its electrons and produce an electrical response. At the time, sufficiently clean samples were difficult to fabricate, preventing researchers from directly testing the prediction. The breakthrough began when Iyengar reexamined experimental data collected with collaborator Manoj Tripathi, now at South Dakota Mines. Their measurements showed unusual electrical signals concentrated around graphene’s sharpest wrinkles. Iyengar brought the findings to Meunier, who had co-advised his doctoral research. “When Sathvik showed me the measurements he and Manoj had collected, we realized that the unusual signals could provide an experimental connection to an idea we had predicted many years earlier,” Meunier said. “I calculated the effect we had predicted for the specific geometry and compared it to the experiment, and it turns out the fit was almost perfect.” To investigate the mechanism, the team combined specialized microscopy, laser measurements, and computer modeling. Microscope probes mapped the wrinkles’ shapes, local electrical energy, and current, while Raman spectroscopy revealed where graphene’s atoms were stretched or compressed. Simulations performed using Penn State’s Roar supercomputer helped predict how extreme bending would influence electrons. Comparing sharply curved wrinkles with nearby flat graphene allowed the researchers to separate the effects of curvature from other influences. The wrinkle tips altered local electrical energy and consistently showed electrical current when approximately one volt was applied. These observations closely matched the team’s calculations and simulations. The wrinkles effectively acted as microscopic obstacles to electrical transport. Their extreme curvature changed the local electronic environment, providing evidence that flexoelectricity can produce a substantial response even in a material only one atom thick. The measured current required an externally applied voltage, so the results do not demonstrate electricity generation without an external power source. The findings point toward a possible method for adjusting the electrical properties of ultrathin materials through precisely controlled bending. Future devices might exploit this behavior to create more sensitive sensors or electronic components whose responses depend on nanoscale geometry. “Nature already creates these tiny wrinkles for us,” Iyengar said. “Understanding how they influence electrical behavior gives scientists another tool for designing future technologies using the structure of a material itself.” Reference: “Sub-Nanometer Curvature Unlocks Quantum Orbital Flexoelectricity in Graphene” by Sathvik Ajay Iyengar, James G. Some of the world’s leading happiness researchers have changed how they live because of what they have discovered. After decades of studying well-being, several have made a conscious effort to spend more time with family and friends, reflecting one of the strongest findings in happiness science. Their insights come from a discussion involving 13 international experts with a combined 600 years of research experience. The conversation, which explored both scientific evidence and personal experience, led to a new paper published in the Journal of Happiness Studies . The key takeaways: “Happiness emerges from a symphony of factors, but if I had to pinpoint one secret to happiness, relationships with other people might be it,” says Lara Aknin, a professor of social psychology at Simon Fraser University. Aknin coauthored the paper with Harvard University’s Säde Stenlund and Kelsey O’Connor, a senior researcher at Luxembourg’s National Institute of Statistics and Economic Studies. She emphasizes that social connections are among the most consistently supported findings in happiness research. “Having relationships is one of the most reliable predictors of happiness that has emerged from a robust body of evidence spanning the social sciences,” says Aknin. “We know that having just one person you can count on is extremely consequential. Having more relationships and more communities that you feel a part of compounds that sense of well-being.” Although genetics and life circumstances influence happiness, researchers emphasize that well-being is not necessarily fixed. People who generally consider themselves happy still experience setbacks, stress, and negative emotions. Their overall well-being can depend partly on how they respond to challenges and the activities they choose to pursue. Some influential models of happiness have estimated that life circumstances, including where someone lives, employment, age, and relationship status, account for roughly 10% of happiness, while voluntary activities may contribute as much as 40%. These figures are model-based estimates rather than fixed proportions that apply to everyone, but they highlight the potential role of personal behavior. “That leaves a lot of opportunity for people who may be more innately pessimistic to start practising research-backed strategies like meditation or gratitude that might help them see the world in a more positive way,” she says. The scientific study of well-being has expanded considerably since the 1970s, when the modern field began taking shape. What was once a relatively small area of research now encompasses numerous approaches to understanding happiness, life satisfaction, social relationships, and psychological health. Aknin, who also coedits the annual World Happiness Report , says this expansion has brought challenges. As researchers pursue increasingly specialized questions, some early leaders worry that the field has become fragmented. Despite these differences, the scientists who participated in the discussion shared a commitment to rigorous research that can be translated into practical ways to improve people’s lives. The researchers also considered how personal well-being affects people’s willingness and ability to support others. Studies have linked happiness with positive outcomes beyond individual life satisfaction, including greater motivation to help other people. “With many large and threatening realities taking place in the world right now, I sometimes worry that the pursuit of happiness can seem trite. But one reason I remain committed to the scientific study of happiness is that happiness in and of itself predicts a number of valuable outcomes, including the motivation to help other people,” she explains. “When people feel they are doing well, they have the ability, the capability, and the motivation to engage in world affairs—to take care of the people they love and take care of their communities.” Aknin describes generosity as a process that can benefit both those who give and those who receive. Supporting others can strengthen relationships and communities, creating opportunities for care and connection to spread. “Generosity is not zero-sum.” Reference: “Reflections on the Past, Present, and Future of Well-Being Science from Several of Its Pioneers” by Säde Stenlund, Kelsey J. Scientists have developed a tiny temperature sensor that harvests energy from magnetic fields near electrical wiring. Electrical wiring produces weak electromagnetic fields that typically go unnoticed, but researchers have found a way to turn some of that energy into a power source for tiny electronic devices. Scientists at the University of Arkansas (U of A) and the University of Michigan have developed a graphene-based energy harvester capable of powering an ultra-low-power temperature sensor without a conventional battery. The prototype operates using energy collected from its immediate surroundings, consuming power measured in nanowatts, or billionths of a watt. It represents another advance toward the team’s goal of developing autonomous sensors that could function unattended for decades. The technology captures energy from magnetic fields generated by electrical wiring carrying alternating current. In the United States, electricity typically operates at 60 hertz, meaning the current changes direction 60 times each second. The researchers designed their sensor to harvest energy from these low-frequency fields. A graphene inductor collects the energy and sends an alternating electrical signal to a custom circuit, which converts it into direct current. That electricity charges capacitors that store energy for the sensor to use. Unlike a battery, a capacitor stores energy in an electric field rather than through chemical reactions. “The inductor adds charge to these capacitors at a slow rate,” explained University of Arkansas physics professor Paul Thibado, “but it’s faster than the rate the sensor uses up the charges from the capacitors.” Because the sensor consumes energy more slowly than the system replenishes it, the capacitors can maintain an electrical reserve. Thibado estimates that this stored energy could keep the device operating for at least 24 hours during a power outage, potentially extending to a week. The new device is the second graphene-powered temperature sensor developed by the research team. Their earlier work demonstrated that graphene-based solar cells could supply enough electricity to operate temperature sensors, establishing another possible source of energy for autonomous electronics. Graphene, a material consisting of a single layer of carbon atoms, has electrical properties that make it useful in energy-harvesting technologies. Thibado has investigated these properties for more than a decade and invented the graphene energy harvesters used in the team’s research. The researchers ultimately want to combine several methods of collecting environmental energy, including sunlight, heat, sound, motion, and ambient electromagnetic fields. A sensor equipped with multiple harvesting systems could continue operating when one energy source becomes unavailable, reducing its dependence on any single power supply. Although temperature measurement provides a practical demonstration, the technology could eventually support sensors used in agriculture, environmental monitoring, medical tracking, wearable electronics, and supply chain management. These applications often require devices to operate in locations where replacing batteries is expensive, inconvenient, or impractical. Thibado describes the long-term vision as “set it and forget it,” with sensors designed to operate for extended periods without routine battery replacement. Eliminating disposable batteries could also reduce maintenance demands and electronic waste, although decades of reliable operation have not yet been demonstrated. The research was published in the Journal of Vacuum Science and Technology B , with MD Rezaul Kabir, a doctoral candidate in materials science and engineering at the University of Arkansas, serving as first author. The project also involves researchers at the University of Michigan, including electrical engineering and computer science professor David Blaauw, whose work focuses on low-power wireless sensors and embedded systems. NTS Innovations, a nanotechnology company, holds the exclusive license to commercialize the graphene energy-harvesting technology. The company has supported patent development, business planning, and efforts to identify potential customers and commercial partners. More than 60 parties have expressed interest in testing the technology and exploring ways to integrate it into products. Ongoing discussions are helping establish practical requirements, including the minimum electrical power needed for different applications. The researchers envision networks of self-powered sensors that can collect information for years with little human intervention. Combining graphene-based energy harvesting with electronics that consume extremely small amounts of electricity could help make that goal achievable, particularly as connected devices become more common in homes, industries, and environmental monitoring systems. Hubble observations of nearby starburst galaxies challenge the idea that supernova winds helped reionize the early universe, suggesting young stars may have enabled radiation to escape before those winds formed. Powerful winds from exploding stars were thought to clear paths for ultraviolet radiation to escape early galaxies. A new study of nearby galaxies suggests those winds may instead make escape more difficult, challenging a leading explanation for how the universe emerged from a fog of neutral hydrogen. Within the first billion years after the Big Bang, that fog made the universe opaque to ultraviolet light. It began to clear during an era called reionization, which started about 13 billion years ago. Energetic radiation from early galaxies struck neutral hydrogen atoms, separating them into charged protons and electrons. “Eventually, when it ionized the majority of hydrogen filling intergalactic space, that was the end of reionization and we see the universe today,” said Cody Carr, a postdoctoral researcher in the Department of Astronomy at the University of Michigan. “We call reionization the last major phase transition of the universe.” For radiation to transform the gas between galaxies, it first had to get out of the galaxies that produced it. Astronomers proposed that supernovae, or large exploding stars, helped by generating winds powerful enough to reshape galaxies and clear routes through the surrounding gas. “Basically, how these galaxies were leaking ionizing radiation isn’t what we thought,” Carr said. Carr led and carried out the study as a postdoctoral scholar at Zhejiang University in China before joining Michigan. The international team, which includes University of Michigan researchers, used the Hubble Space Telescope to observe nearby starburst galaxies, where stars form at exceptionally high rates. These galaxies resemble some of those thought to have helped reionize the early universe, giving researchers a way to investigate how radiation escapes. The team analyzed the galaxies’ spectra, which separate their light into different wavelengths, to measure the speeds of their galactic winds. Gas moving in those winds absorbs light at specific wavelengths, leaving dips whose positions and widths reveal how the gas is moving. Galaxies with the fastest winds allowed the smallest fraction of ionizing radiation to escape. “It appears that energy input from supernovae has stirred up the surroundings and increased, rather than decreased, the coverage of neutral gas and dust that suppresses ionizing radiation escape,” said Stephan McCandliss, a senior author of the study and director of the Center for Astrophysical Sciences at Johns Hopkins University. The findings, published in Nature Astronomy , strengthen an alternative explanation centered on activity from young stars. Radiation and smaller winds operating in the neighborhoods of these stars could help light escape. “Our observations show that these photons are escaping before galactic winds form,” Carr said. The researchers are working to secure more Hubble observing time to examine additional galaxies and further test the role of these smaller winds. Hubble is a NASA mission launched with contributions from the European Space Agency. The telescope also supported the study through a grant administered by the Space Telescope Science Institute. Connecting the behavior of nearby galaxies to the universe’s early transformation remains an unfinished task. “We don’t know exactly what objects caused reionization or how it evolved,” Carr said. “We know that it took place, but we don’t have complete answers to those questions.” The observations can already inform computer simulations that astronomers use to investigate reionization, particularly how stellar activity changes the gas through which radiation must travel. “Supernovae play a central role in cosmological hydrodynamic simulations that explain how ionizing radiation escapes from galaxies,” said Renyue Cen, a senior author of the study and professor and director of the Center for Cosmology and Computational Astrophysics at Zhejiang University. “Our findings highlight the need to examine how radiation and winds from young stars shape the surrounding gas before the first supernovae explode.” Reference: “Lyman continuum escape during the onset of galactic winds in compact starbursts” by Cody Carr, Renyue Cen, Stephan McCandliss, Jack Ford, Alberto Saldana-Lopez, Claudia Scarlata, Mason S. This positioning influences which regulatory elements can interact with genes and control their activity. “The genome isn’t just a sequence of genes. It’s folded into a complex three-dimensional structure,” said lead author Dr. Thea Rogers. “Understanding how that structure evolves is becoming increasingly important for understanding how new forms of biological complexity arise.” By examining genome architecture alongside gene activity in octopuses, squid, and cuttlefish, the researchers identified the lasting effects of a major evolutionary restructuring. DNA regions that were previously separated became neighbors, creating opportunities for new regulatory interactions. Astronomers have discovered an unusual planet with an extremely hot host star and a highly eccentric orbit that challenges expectations for its class. A giant planet racing around an unusually hot star has caught astronomers’ attention because of its highly elongated orbit. Known as TOI-1355 b, the planet completes one revolution in roughly two Earth days, following a path that differs sharply from the nearly circular orbits typical of many hot Jupiters. Researchers from the University of Tokyo and their international collaborators believe the planet’s unusual trajectory could help explain how giant planets migrate toward their stars. Although astronomers have discovered thousands of planets around stars similar to or cooler than the Sun, planetary systems surrounding hotter stars remain less thoroughly explored. Project Researcher Noriharu Watanabe and Professor Norio Narita of the University of Tokyo’s Graduate School of Arts and Sciences are investigating these systems to better understand the diversity of planets beyond our solar system. “Planet surveys around stars as hot or cooler than the sun are flourishing, and thousands of planets have been discovered around such stars. But planet surveys around hotter stars are still not advanced,” said Watanabe. “In this project, we hunted for planets around hot stars to examine the diversity of exoplanets more broadly. When we investigated the change in brightness of TOI-1355 from prior data, we found that the secondary eclipse, a phenomenon in which a planet passes behind a star, occurred faster than the timing assumed for a circular orbit. The researchers also examined the secondary eclipse, when the planet passes behind its star. Its unexpected timing indicated that TOI-1355 b was traveling along an elliptical rather than circular orbit. Calculating the mass required more complex mathematical models to account for the planet’s elongated trajectory. One possible explanation for TOI-1355 b’s orbit involves gravitational encounters with other massive planets or celestial bodies. James Webb Space Telescope observations suggest that exotic mineral clouds may be shielding a distant lava planet from its star. A rocky planet exposed to extreme heat from its star appears to reflect nearly three-quarters of the starlight that reaches it. Astronomers suspect silicate-mineral clouds could act as a protective sunscreen, helping the planet maintain temperatures far below those expected for an exposed surface of molten rock. The planet, TOI-561 b, lies about 280 light-years from Earth and was previously considered too hot to retain a substantial atmosphere. New observations from the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) suggest that it has a significant envelope of gas that reflects incoming radiation and redistributes heat around the planet. The findings, published in The Astronomical Journal , challenge existing theories about how atmospheres survive on intensely irradiated rocky worlds. An international research team, including University of Birmingham astrophysicist Dr. Anjali Piette, monitored TOI-561 b for 37 hours, covering nearly four complete orbits around its star. By measuring changes in the planet’s brightness and thermal emission throughout its orbit, the researchers investigated how heat is distributed between its permanently illuminated dayside and its dark nightside. Earlier observations had shown that the dayside was unexpectedly cool for a bare, dark rocky surface. Scientists considered whether winds might be transporting the missing heat to the nightside or whether the planet was reflecting much of the incoming starlight. Webb’s first measurements of the nightside showed that it was not warm enough to account for the difference. The results indicate that TOI-561 b reflects approximately 75% of the starlight it receives, a proportion comparable to Venus. Professor Lisa Dang, the project’s lead researcher at the University of Waterloo in Ontario, Canada, explained: “We measured how the planet’s brightness and heat changed throughout its orbit. This technique, known as a phase curve, revealed that the planet reflects a significant amount of light from its star, and that heat is being redistributed around the planet instead of only on the sunlit side. Together, these point to the presence of an atmosphere.” To investigate the planet’s unusual reflectivity, the researchers compared their measurements with computer simulations of its climate. The models suggest that clouds containing silicate minerals, including silicon dioxide (SiO2) and magnesium silicate (MgSiO3), could form on the dayside. These clouds might reflect substantial amounts of stellar radiation before it can heat the surface, much as a sunscreen reduces the amount of sunlight absorbed by skin. The atmosphere’s chemical composition remains unknown. One possibility is a dense layer of carbon dioxide, resembling the atmosphere of Venus but exposed to much more extreme conditions. Another is an atmosphere rich in sulfur dioxide, a volcanic gas also released by Jupiter’s moon Io. Neither scenario would produce habitable conditions. The evidence for a substantial atmosphere raises questions about the planet’s history. Intense stellar radiation should have stripped much of the gas from a rocky world like TOI-561 b over billions of years. Yet the new measurements strengthen earlier findings suggesting that the planet still possesses a thick atmosphere, potentially replenished by gases escaping from its molten interior. Dr. Piette, Assistant Professor in Astronomy at the University of Birmingham, said: “Our discovery challenges current theories. We would expect a heavily irradiated rocky planet like TOI-561 b to have lost its atmosphere billions of years ago.” “Instead, the evidence suggests it still has a significant atmosphere today. This raises major questions such as whether the planet started with an unusually large supply of gases or if the ocean of molten rock covering its surface, acts as a planet-wide volcano that is constantly feeding its atmosphere.” Determining which gases surround TOI-561 b could help researchers understand how its atmosphere has persisted under such extreme conditions. Professor Dang added: “The next big question we will seek to answer is whether TOI-561 b’s atmosphere resembles Venus or an extreme version of Io. This capacity for rapid adaptation could help them cope with environmental change, including climate change,” says Cumer. The team now plans to use computer analysis of photographs to measure color and spotting more precisely. Researchers also intend to reconstruct the plumage color of birds that died very young using their genetic data, allowing them to investigate whether particular plumage features are associated with better chances of survival. The extraordinary intelligence of octopuses, squid, and cuttlefish may be linked to more than just their genes. Octopuses can solve problems, squid can rapidly change their appearance, and cuttlefish display remarkably sophisticated behaviors. These abilities rely on unusually complex nervous systems, but how such biological complexity evolved remains an open question. A new study suggests that part of the answer may lie in the three-dimensional structure of DNA rather than in genes alone. Scientists at the University of Vienna discovered evidence that extensive genome rearrangements hundreds of millions of years ago changed how different regions of DNA interact in cephalopods. Published in Nature Communications , the study suggests that these ancient changes may have helped establish new patterns of gene regulation, potentially contributing to the evolution of their elaborate nervous systems. DNA is not arranged as a straight strand inside the cell nucleus. Instead, it folds into a complex three-dimensional structure that brings distant genetic regions close together. This positioning influences which regulatory elements can interact with genes and control their activity. “The genome isn’t just a sequence of genes. It’s folded into a complex three-dimensional structure,” said lead author Dr. Thea Rogers. “Understanding how that structure evolves is becoming increasingly important for understanding how new forms of biological complexity arise.” By examining genome architecture alongside gene activity in octopuses, squid, and cuttlefish, the researchers identified the lasting effects of a major evolutionary restructuring. DNA regions that were previously separated became neighbors, creating opportunities for new regulatory interactions. Over time, some of these connections may have developed into increasingly interconnected networks, a process the researchers describe as “regulatory entanglement.” The study also found that different levels of genome organization have evolved at strikingly different rates. Large structural regions called chromatin domains remained relatively stable over evolutionary time, even as other features of the genome changed substantially. Smaller structures known as chromatin loops showed much greater variation across species, tissues, and developmental stages. These loops bring distant sections of DNA into physical proximity, allowing regulatory elements to influence genes that may be far away along the DNA sequence. Many occurred near genes associated with distinctive cephalopod characteristics, including those linked to the nervous system. The researchers propose that regulatory entanglement may allow genomes to develop new patterns of gene expression while preserving essential biological functions. Stable chromatin domains could help maintain existing regulatory organization, while more flexible loops provide opportunities for evolutionary changes. The findings suggest that the physical arrangement of DNA may actively influence evolutionary processes rather than simply reflect changes that have already occurred. title: ‘It’s big’: Astronomers make startling discovery of a possible dwarf planet beyond Pluto
content: Astronomers have spotted a new dwarf planet candidate in the solar system, beyond the orbit of Pluto, which they provisionally named ED138. If future observations confirm the discovery, ED138 will join a group currently made up of five dwarf planets that have been recognized by the International Astronomical Union, or IAU: Ceres, Pluto, Haumea, Makemake and Eris. The finding is the result of detections made by the Vera C. Rubin Observatory, a new telescope that sits atop a 2,682-meter-tall (8,800-foot-tall) mountain in Chile and houses the world’s largest digital camera. The telescope started operating in 2025 and is capable of imaging the entire sky every three days. Matthew Holman, a Smithsonian senior astrophysicist and lecturer in astronomy at Harvard University, ran a computer program he codeveloped to comb through data collected by Rubin earlier in 2026, scanning billions of detections of moving objects. When ED138 popped up, Holman said he first reacted with “excited disbelief,” and immediately checked for a false positive or an error with the computer program. To confirm the observation, Holman, who is also a Rubin Operations team member, worked with his colleague Mario Jurić, the Rubin Solar System lead scientist and a professor in the department of astronomy at the University of Washington. Jurić looked for more observations of ED138 in Rubin’s catalog, and found 20 additional ones dating back to March 2026. Eventually, using other sources, the researchers were able to plot the orbit of the object as far back as 10 years. However, Holman warns, ED138 isn’t officially a dwarf planet yet: “At this point, it’s still a candidate. We really need to know how physically big it is, and that will take a few months, probably.” ED138’s diameter is estimated to be between 600 and 1,500 kilometers (370 and 930 miles), which would make it bigger than the smallest of the recognized dwarf planets, Ceres. It currently orbits the sun at a distance of about 46 astronomical units — with each unit representing the average distance between Earth and the sun. That means ED138 is farther away than Pluto and also a trans-Neptunian object, or TNO — a class of objects that orbit the sun at a distance greater than Neptune’s. In the night sky, ED138 is not visible with the naked eye but “is bright enough that really capable amateurs can see it if they know where to look,” according to Holman. Part of the reason scientists hadn’t discovered ED138 before is because it’s in the southern hemisphere, and therefore very difficult to observe from the northern hemisphere, Holman noted. “That already rules out whole sets of telescopes that might have found this, and there aren’t as many telescopes searching the sky in the southern hemisphere,” he said. Another factor that kept ED138 hidden is that it is on the same plane as our galaxy. “For the last 20 years, the object has kind of been looping its way across the Milky Way, from our point of view ,” Holman explained. “People don’t typically search for things in the Milky Way, because there’s so many stars that it’s really hard to find moving objects.” The new dwarf planet candidate joins the Rubin telescope’s growing list of detected objects — largely asteroids and much smaller TNOs. According to Holman, there might be “a handful” more objects the size of ED138, and Rubin should eventually find those, too. “Rubin Observatory is just doing its job really well, inventorying the Solar System to new depths,” said Megan Schwamb, a reader in astrophysics at Queen’s University Belfast and a member of the Rubin Solar System Operations team, in an email. “I was surprised that it found such an object so early in the commissioning observations. This was not on my bingo card for this year,” Schwamb added. “It shows how Rubin’s combination of speed, depth, and sky coverage is going to transform our view of the Solar System over the next decade and especially in the next few years.” In 2006, the IAU adopted a new definition of planet, describing it as an object that orbits the sun, is mostly round, and is big enough that it has cleared its orbit of objects of similar size. Scientists made the controversial decision to demote Pluto, because it didn’t satisfy the last requirement, and our solar system went from nine to eight planets. At the same time, Pluto and its ilk became known as dwarf planets — nearly round objects that orbit the sun but aren’t large enough to have cleared their own orbits of debris. If ED138 is confirmed as a new dwarf planet, astronomers will first give it a permanent number and then an actual name, although the process could take time, and the details of who exactly will get to choose the name are still unclear. “People have already emailed me some suggestions, and some of them are already taken by other objects,” Holman said. “I don’t know. It’ll be fun. Maybe I’ll get to suggest something, but I’m not going to hold my breath, because this is a big, big project.” The finding is significant for the field, said Michele Bannister, an associate professor at the University of Canterbury in New Zealand, who was not involved with the discovery of ED138. The object is “scientifically really cool because it’s a trans-Neptunian object and it’s also physically quite large, but still a lot fainter than you can see with the naked eye,” said Bannister, who studies the small worlds of the solar system. The size of the object is just within the range where we can start to think of it as a world, she added, and other telescopes will now pick up the baton to find out more about it. “Maybe if we ever fly a spacecraft there, we’ll find it has a nitrogen glacier like Pluto,” Bannister said. “That would be great to see. But at the moment, all we know is that it’s big, and the rest is going to be speculation for a little bit, about what its physical characteristics really are.”

title: A painting went missing 20 years ago. Police tracked it down with the help of AI
content:
Art theft is a global problem and police forces are struggling to keep on top of it. Now they are turning to AI software that snoop out the most cleverly hidden artworks.
During their routine visit to the annual antiquity fair in Parma , Italy, in October 2024, police officers busily snapped photos of the artworks as they walked between the stands. It wasn't art appreciation – it was detective work.
The images were uploaded to an internal database as the officers smiled at the vendors and wandered amid fist-sized bronze statuettes, patinated goblets, yellowing globes, and an endless assortment of oil paintings.
Just a couple of hours later, though, the police system flagged one of the snapshots with an alert signal: a painting of a young, fair-skinned woman wearing aquamarine and red, holding up a half-unravelled parchment scroll.
The next day, officers rushed to the scene and seized the painting for their art experts to take a second look. The scroll in the painting was now, indeed, giving the investigators reason to be suspicious, says Lt Col Salvatore Rapicavoli, of the police unit for the Protection of Cultural Heritage of Italy. "There was something off."
While Rapicavoli's team has specialised in tracking down stolen artworks nationwide for decades, he says that the novel, tailor-made artificial i ntelligence system they were testing at the fair has massively sharpened their craft. It has since allowed the team to detect stolen art more quickly and helped them to spot details beyond what the human eye can normally see.
"There has been an exponential increase in the number of hits," says Rapicavoli. Since its introduction in November 2023, the AI system has helped his team recover more than 300 large plundered paintings and statues, and more than 165,000 smaller coins, medals, letters, manuscripts, religious objects, stamps and cards worth more than a total of €203m (£170m, $226m). The advances in Italy – in technique and policy – have been paving the way for machine learning in art theft investigations worldwide , promising to revolutionise the global crackdown on art heisters.
And while a human would likely have glossed over that woman holding a parchment scroll at first glance – nothing but a couple of darker shadows looking off balance – the team now had an active investigation on their hands.
Since 1969, the Italian police have kept a database of looted cultural artefacts across the nation – everything from gigantic oil paintings ripped from church altars in the night to ancient Roman and Etruscan artefacts excavated illegally. The database – the largest in the world, constantly fed by reports from cultural police authorities and customs – contains more than one million items. Though only some of the entries have pictures of the original artefacts.
Historically, to find stolen artworks, Italian police routinely visited fairs, antique shops, and upscale art auctions and compared what they saw there with millions of records back in their offices, first in paper form, then digitised in an online database. One by one, they would look for matches in the online repository by searching keywords, querying with details like "painting of woman with scroll".
This was time-consuming and clumsy, though, says Rapicavoli. Even if a sale looked suspicious, an officer scrolling through hundreds of database photos for a match could often miss key details. And the quality of the original artefact photos left a lot to be desired. The images were often taken decades earlier, in black and white, far away, on someone's dining room wall and littered with light blowouts, obscured areas, or extreme contrast.
"I asked myself how technology could get around this problem," says Rapicavoli, an IT engineer who joined the Italian police's stolen art team in 2013. "At least in the massive search-and-comparison phase."
In 2020, his team conceived the AI algorithm called the Stolen Works of Art Detection System (Swoads). "The machine doesn't get bored," says Rapicavoli. Crucially, it can match hidden visual fingerprints in the works – pairing similarities between shades of colour and rough silhouettes.
It can also spot segments of paintings that have been chopped up and rearranged – as is often the case with large altarpieces sold in separate slivers – or works that have been tweaked after being stolen. "Regardless of whether it makes sense or not, it recognises it because it's part of a whole that was stolen," says Rapicavoli. It can reconcile the art without truly knowing its meaning or content.
A manual search for a painting of a "woman with a scroll" in the stolen artworks database wouldn't have solved the case on Rapicavoli's hands. The keywords wouldn't have surfaced the painting stolen 20 years earlier, in which that same fair-skinned woman clutches a small white lamb and a palm branch instead of a scroll.
Because the AI had spotted the similarities in colour, pattern and set-up – irrespective of the missing scroll – it flagged it among millions of stolen artefacts despite the manner of its disguise. Once it fetched the source image it believed it resembled, the similarities to the human eye were immediately apparent.
In fact, a closer investigation confirmed that a 17th-Century, 1m-tall (3.3ft) painting of Saint Agnese had been looted from the small church of Virgo Potens in Sulmona, near Naples, over 500km (310 miles) from the Parma art fair, on the night of 11 August 2004. It had apparently then been painted over to appear less recognisable – the lamb now the scroll, and the halo and the palm branch erased to turn the Saint into a young pagan woman instead.
As the art trade moved from in-person auctions to online marketplaces, Rapicavoli's team was finding itself constantly playing catch-up with a flurry of new uploads across e-commerce platforms, social media, and even the dark web. Now Swoads can continuously crawl catalogues and new uploads day and night, constantly scraping the internet and comparing millions of images against a stolen-art database.
In 2026, for instance, the same software allowed his team in the Italian city of Turin to recover a painting by Filippo Palizzi, Riposo Della Pastorella (The Rest of the Shephardess), stolen from a modern art gallery in June 1972, in a robbery so severe the establishment remained shut down for over 30 years.
Although the painting had been missing for decades, lost in the backrooms of art markets and trade shows, one of its routine trawls of the internet spotted it for sale on an auction house website.
